plans.objective: [DIM: optimization] The minimal network width $N_c(w)$ required to achieve zero violation on held-out constraints is non-decreasing in $w$ for rigid families due to the rank of the constraint Jacobian, while for fat families it diverges as the constraint manifold becomes underspecified. | pro: Grounds the problem in the geometry of the loss landscape; directly relates to the monotonicity observed in prior iterations. con: The optimization landscape of small networks is non-convex and initialization-sensitive; a failure to find a solution may reflect local minima rather than true solution space fatness. |

steps.description: Implement a numerical experiment in Python to test the hypothesis that $N_c(w)$ (minimum width for zero violation) is non-decreasing in $w$ for rigid families and diverges for fat families. Define rigid family as a linear system $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with full-rank $A$ (unique solution), and fat family as an underdetermined system with rank-deficient $A$ (infinite solutions). Use a 2-layer MLP with ReLU activation, He initialization, and Adam optimizer. Train on both constraint sets, sweep hidden width $N \in [10, 500]$ and constraint counts $w \in [5, 100]$, measure max absolute error on held-out constraints, and determine $N_c(w)$ at threshold $\leq 10^{-3}$. Address non-convexity by using 10 random initializations per configuration and selecting the best result. Include convergence checks and divergence detection for fat families.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The constraint system defines a linear subspace of dimension d = n - w, and a two-layer ReLU network of width N_c(w) = d can exactly represent any solution if the hidden layer spans the solution subspace, implying N_c(w) is finite and independent of w (rigid).

steps.description: We will design and run a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the solution space of a constraint system admits a low-dimensional linear/algebraic structure, evidenced by $N_c(w)$ (minimum network width for zero violation) remaining bounded as $w$ (constraint count) increases. Results will include $N_c(w)$ values, training/validation error curves, and scaling trends.

steps.description: [auto-routed: surprise=1.00] This workflow tests the logarithmic scaling hypothesis by reformulating the constraint system to respect the low-dimensional manifold geometry. Steps: (1) Generate a 2D torus manifold embedded in 3D ambient space using intrinsic coordinates $(\theta, \phi) \in [0, 2\pi]^2$; (2) Define the constraint system as the two intrinsic embedding equations $f_1(x) = 0, f_2(x) = 0$ that define the torus surface (fixed geometry, independent of $w$); (3) Sample $w$ distinct points uniformly on the manifold to form a training set (no interpolation required); (4) Train MLPs to minimize the residual norm $\sum_{j=1}^2 \|f_j(x_{pred})\|^2$; (5) Measure zero violation as the max projection error $\max_{x \in \text{test}} \text{dist}(x, \text{Manifold}) \le 10^{-3}$; (6) Determine $N_c(w)$ as the minimal width achieving this threshold on held-out test points and fit the scaling law. This isolates the intrinsic dimensionality (2) from ambient dimension (3) and sampling density ($w$).

plans.objective: [DIM: dynamics] The solution space of the constraint system admits a low-dimensional manifold structure such that the minimal width $N_c(w)$ saturates to a constant as $w$ increases, indicating a rigid solution space where small networks can generalize to unseen constraints without increasing capacity.

steps.description: Systematically scan the parameter space of constraint systems (w, dimensionality, functional form) and network architectures (width, depth, activation) to measure N_c(w) and test the saturation hypothesis. This includes: (1) generating constraint families with varying intrinsic manifold dimensionality; (2) training small feedforward networks with varying hidden widths; (3) measuring the minimum width N_c required to achieve zero violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraints; (4) plotting N_c vs. w to identify saturation. If saturation is not observed, analyze whether the solution space is "fat" (high-dimensional) or if network capacity/optimization is the bottleneck.
